title: Sent (Acts 13:1–3)
hookLine: while they fast and pray, Barnabas and Saul are set apart

cards: Three verses. That's all Luke spends on the moment that starts the great journeys of Paul, the ones that carried the gospel across the Mediterranean. No vision on a road this time, no earthquake, no angel.
Just a church in Antioch doing something ordinary: worshiping, and going without food.

teach.b: Luke bothers to list the names. In the church at Antioch there are prophets and teachers: Barnabas. Simeon, who was called Niger, a Latin nickname meaning dark or black.
Lucius of Cyrene, from North Africa. Manaen, who had been brought up with Herod the tetrarch, the same Herod who killed John the Baptist. And Saul, the former persecutor.
A Cypriot, likely an African or two, a man raised in a royal court, and a converted enemy: that's the leadership.
As they minister to the Lord and fast, the Holy Spirit speaks, paraphrased here: set apart for me Barnabas and Saul, for the work to which I have called them.
The Greek word for set apart means to mark off, to separate for a purpose. Paul later begins his letter to the Romans calling himself separated for the gospel of God, the same root.
And the church doesn't send them off at once. It fasts and prays again. Then they lay their hands on the two men, and send them away.
The church let go of two of its five best teachers. Sending costs something.
Catholics see a pattern here that the Church still follows: prayer and fasting before big decisions, and the laying on of hands to mark someone sent for a task, as in ordination today.
And notice who speaks first in this story: not a committee, but the Spirit, heard by people who had made a little quiet by going without.

how: Catholics fast on Ash Wednesday and Good Friday and abstain from meat on Lenten Fridays, many add small fasts of their own, and in ordination the bishop lays his hands on the one being ordained in silence.

s: Paul's journeys began with a vision on a road
they began in a church at Antioch that was worshiping and fasting.
the church fasted and prayed again before sending them
then they laid hands on them and sent them away.
Antioch's leaders all came from one place
Cyprus, Cyrene, a royal court, and Tarsus: Luke lists them.

games.q: you're the church at Antioch. the Spirit says to set apart two of your five best teachers. what do you do?
o: fast and pray again, lay hands on them, and send them.
keep one; the church needs him.
games.why: they fast and pray once more, lay their hands on Barnabas and Saul, and let them go.

practice: Picture one small thing you could go without, the phone at meals, the second coffee, the background noise in the car, and the gap it would leave; that gap is the kind of room the church in Antioch prayed in.
In the quiet you have right now, ask what you might be set apart for: not a mission across the sea, maybe a person, a task, a conversation. If you pray, offer that small fast and simply listen.

wordCard.voice: Sent. Barnabas and Saul, set apart while the church fasted and prayed, given the laying on of hands, and let go. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: set apart, mark off for a purpose. the root behind Paul calling himself separated for the gospel.

carryVoice: Your line: set apart. Tomorrow, a hard question, and a council to settle it. See you there.
